title: From Paper to Pixels: How I Built a Digital Companion for My Fountain Pen & Ink Journal
content:
For years, whenever I inked up a fountain pen, I reached for my paper journal. My current companion is an Endless stationery notebook with dotted Tomoe River paper. Every time a new pen-and-ink pairing came together, I would jot down the date, the pen, the nib size, and the ink. Whenever I was ready to ink up a pen, I’d flip through earlier pages to pick an ink or check how a nib performed. There is something deeply satisfying about writing on Tomoe River paper—the sheen, the shading, the feel of the nib gliding across smooth paper. That ritual isn’t going anywhere; I still log every single fill on paper by hand.

Over time, though, questions kept popping up that paper made tricky to answer: Which inks haven't I inked up in over a year? How many pens are currently inked in the rotation? What was the last pen I paired with that specific bottle of green? And how much paper and notebook inventory do I actually have left in the cabinet? I wanted a quick, effortless way to explore those answers without thumbing back through dozens of notebook pages.

Bringing Paper into Pixels

So I built Atelier Ink & Nib—a dedicated digital companion for my collection. It tracks everything in one place:

  • Currently inked pens (and how long each has been inked)
  • Complete pen and nib specs, alongside photos of my actual pens
  • Ink bottles and sample vials, with color swatches and usage logs
  • Notebook and loose-sheet paper inventory
  • Historical inking sessions and handwriting samples

Uncovering Forgotten Favorites & Collection Stats

Having all the historical logs digitized surfaced some fascinating insights into my own pen and ink habits over the years:

  • All-Time Most-Inked Pens: The Pilot Vanishing Point (Blue Matte) leads the pack with 14 inking sessions, followed closely by the Canary Yellow Vanishing Point (11 fills) and the classic Lamy 2000 (11 fills).
  • My Go-To Workhorse Ink: Diamine Turquoise took top honors with 8 separate fills across different pens.
  • The Forgotten Favorites: The data revealed that inks like Diamine Turquoise, Noodler's Black Swan in Australian Roses, and Rohrer & Klingner Salix—along with pens like my Sailor 1911 and Pilot Falcon—were in heavy rotation up through mid-2023, but haven't been inked once since! Seeing that clearly in the dashboard gave me the immediate urge to bring them back into the active pen case.

Accurate Ink Colors & Respecting Community Creators

One of my favorite touches is how ink shades are represented. Digital swatches rarely do fountain pen inks justice—they can’t easily convey shading, sheen, or wetness. For every ink in my cabinet, I added a direct reference link to its review on the wonderful Mountain of Ink blog by Kelli.

Out of respect for copyright, I haven't scraped or copied any of her swatch images into my tool, but having a one-click jump directly to her exhaustive reviews and writing samples gives me the perfect visual reference whenever I’m deciding what to ink next.

Pair-Programming with AI as a Software Engineer

As a software engineer, I write code every day, but for a personal hobby project, I didn't want to get bogged down in weeks of boilerplate, schema wiring, and data entry. Instead, I used AI as an active pair-programming partner.

We brainstormed the database structure together, drafted the interface, and rapidly wired up the components. What would have taken weeks of after-hours tinkering came together smoothly in just a few focused sessions—letting me spend less time wrestling with code and more time enjoying the collection.

The Best of Both Worlds

The digital dashboard doesn’t replace my paper journal—it enhances it. The analog ritual stays untouched, but now I have an instant bird’s-eye view of my collection whenever I’m planning my next pen-and-ink combination.
